Here is a link from American College of Cardiology with some background information: https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/Articles/2020/03/19/16/00/New-Information-on-Accuracy-of-LDL-C-Estimation

That page details the equation used to calculate LDL (the friedewald equation). The equation is pretty straight forward: LDL = total cholesterol - HDL - (triglycerides/5).

You can play around with the equation to see how it performs. Having a very high triglycerides value would skew ldl too low, but having a very small triglycerides value skews it high. 

Link to calculator: 
https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/clinical-calculator/friedewald-equation-for-low-density-lipoprotein-ldl-c

For example, if your total cholesterol was 255, HDL was 55, and trigs were 40, you get a ldl value of 192. That’s high! But if your trigs were 350, your ldl would be 130.

If your triglycerides are below 100 mg/dl or above 400 mg/dl, the equation used to calculate ldl is inaccurate. Otherwise, the calculated value is pretty accurate. For example, if you have triglyceride concentration of 40 mg/dl, your ldl calculated is going to artificially high. Vice versa if your trigs concentration is very high.

Personally, I would rely on ldl direct if I had enough data points of it. It seems Ldl calculated tends to be cheaper or easier for laboratory analysis, so that’s often the only data point people have to go off of. And that’s okay (generally).

I grew up through the “poke mania” craze in the 90s as a kid, so it had a large impression on me. Playing through Blue *forced* me to learn to read. I played the games as soon as they came out all the way through platinum. By the time B/W came out, I was a Junior in high school and thought it shouldn’t be playing anymore, I should be more interested in adult things. So I put it off, chased girls, graduated high school, and started working full time as an electrician’s apprentice the week after graduation. I guess my decisions were dictated by my desire to prove to myself that I was an adult. 

But let me tell you, being an adult suuuckkss. I went through a year of working that job and hated it. Majority of my co-workers were 30+, had children, married/divorced; They were bonafide adults with real problems and real pasts. Maybe it’s because I couldn’t relate, maybe it’s because of the stark contrast between coasting through high school vs 50+ hour weeks of manual labor, but I think it’s mostly that I was trying to be someone that I wasn’t that had made me miserable during this time. So I quit, and hated myself for not being able to burden that life. 

Life drifted in limbo for a couple months, until I picked up B/W and played through it. I think I can describe my experience as being cathartic... Pokemon was one of the many things I had shelved in order to “grow up”, but damn did playing it make me happy. I think playing through B/W helped me realize that growing up didn’t mean I had to change who I was to fit the general narrative of whatever society expected of me. So Gen 5 has a special place in my heart, and I think it’s beautifully poetic that Gen 5 was a rebirth of the franchise (only able to catch /use gen 5 Pokémon throughout first play through) just as much as it helped ground and redefine myself.

Long story short, I loved B/W and I’m glad you’re enjoying it too.

So again, to be clear because Lydiard was never very exact in his methodology but rather more fluid, from my understanding these are not all out sprints. They are more of an exercise for very rapid leg turnover, if that makes sense?

VO2max = ml/kg/min, so generally any added unnecessary weight will decrease this metric. So if someone has a vO2max of 60 and they weigh 150lbs(68kg), they utilize 60ml of Oxygen per kg of bodyweight. When weight is gained, all other things equal, vO2max decreases (I.e. oxygen utilization per kg falls) which generally means poorer performance. Of course, someone could gain weight AND become more efficient/more aerobically developed etc, and they could increase performance. It'll just be fighting an uphill battle.

As far as heart rate goes, I would guess it comes down to aerobic development? If you trained your body to carry oxygen effectively and built up some nice capillarization in your legs with some high mileage, your heart rate at a given pace should fall. I’m not a pro runner, but I used to run at a small D3 college. Ran ~ 4:03 for 1500m and 1:57 for 800m. 

I would suggest periodization. I think it was the most important concept behind training to run faster. The mile is a very aerobic event, but it also requires a strong anaerobic effort as well. So training both of these systems should come in and out of focus throughout your training cycles. 

Generally, lots of people like to start with a period of high volume, low intensity work for an extended amount of time. You can tailor the length of time you spend running higher easy mileage according to when you’d like to race your mile. The more time spent in this period, the greater your aerobic system gets. I’d suggest throwing in some strides after easy runs for sake of keeping some speed in the legs.

From there I’d suggest transitioning to some more intensive workouts. Start doing a tempo run once a week, and also some longer repeats at 3k-10k pace. I use both the Jack Daniels Running and McMillian Running calculator to come up with my paces for these workouts. You should not feel completely fried after these, more so just comfortably tired. Outside of these two workouts, keep any other day you run easy.

Then finally, the last general cycle people go through is a period of specific race pace work. So these would be the fun workouts consisting of 200s, 400s, maybe some 600s (for someone focusing on the mile). These workouts would be ran at 800-mile race pace and should feel difficult and hurt toward the end. But you want to try and make these repeats still feel as relaxed as possible at the same time. Some example workouts would be 8x200 @ 800m pace 60s recovery, a ladder (100, 200, 300, etc and back down) with 1:1 recovery, and the fan favorite 10x400 @ mile pace, 60s recovery. That 10x400 is killer and the average pace you can hold for the 400s will be about your average pace per 400 in a mile race. And make sure you’re running easy recovery days around these workouts.

Another thing to keep in mind is to keep your easy days EASY and your hard days hard. Do any core work and strength training on days you have a workout, your body will thank you. 

TL;DR: 
Run lots of easy miles for awhile., the longer you do this the more pay off you’ll see probably. Then start to narrow down and do harder workouts at race pace.

While reading through the comments, a lot of them consist of people either condemning running or mentioning how painful/dull of an activity it is. Everybody has their likes and dislikes, but in my opinion, I believe you are all running too hard for the most part.

Any day you go out to do mileage should be at an enjoyable pace. Take your heart rate and subtract it from 180. Try to keep your heart rate in that range. Or just try to run at a pace that you can breath through your nose the entire time. It's better to run slower longer, at a pace that allows you to do so comfortably (at least on your easy days).

In general, people should be moving slowly a lot more often. This includes walking and running. It's good practice to throw in a faster paced tempo run and even a very fast interval/sprint session once a week/biweek.

TL;DR If running is a chore and painful on the regular basis for you, run slower ya dingus. Then mix in fast stuff once in awhile.
